How to Prepare for Postpartum: Make a Plan Before Birth

Updated: August 26, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

To prepare for postpartum, write a one-page plan in your third trimester that covers who will help, how the baby will be fed, how each adult will sleep, what to stock at home, and when you will see your own provider. Think of it as the postpartum counterpart to a birth plan, made while you can still think clearly. This guide walks through each section of that plan in order, with targets you can actually hit before week 38.

Write a one-page postpartum plan

A birth plan covers one day. A postpartum plan covers the six weeks after it, and those weeks are usually harder to improvise. Sometime between week 32 and week 36, sit down for an hour and write one page that answers five questions: who is helping, how the baby will be fed, how each adult will get sleep, what the house needs to have on hand, and when you will see your own provider. You are not trying to predict everything. You are making the easy decisions now so that nobody has to make them at 3 a.m. while holding a newborn.

Keep the plan short enough to fit on one page, and put it somewhere the whole household can see it, like the fridge or a shared note. Share a copy with your partner and anyone on your support list so the plan does not live only in your head. It also helps to keep a running list of dates, questions for your provider, and things you notice, in BeMama or a paper notebook, so the details are in one place when appointments come around. Treat the plan as a draft. You will adjust it in the first week, and that is a sign it is being used, not that it failed.

Name your support roster and visitor rules

Vague offers of help evaporate under a crying baby, so turn them into names and jobs now. Write down who covers dinner on which nights, who runs a load of laundry when they visit, who takes older kids to school or the park, and who walks the dog. People generally like being given a specific job, and asking before the birth is much easier than asking from the couch afterward. If your list is short, that is worth knowing early too. A neighbor, a meal train, a grocery delivery subscription, or a few weeks of paid help can stand in for family who live far away.

Decide on visitor rules while you can still think about them calmly. Some families want a full house in week one; many want two quiet weeks first. Common rules that work well: visits are short, visitors wash their hands, nobody comes while sick, and anyone who stays longer than twenty minutes does a chore. Agree on the rules with your partner and pick who delivers the message, so one of you is not stuck enforcing limits alone. A simple line covers most situations: we would love to see you, and we will reach out when we are ready for visitors.

Plan feeding and sleep before you are exhausted

Whatever way you hope to feed your baby, write down your plan A and a plan B you can live with. If you want to breastfeed or chestfeed, find your lactation support contact now: a lactation consultant, a clinic line, a public health nurse, or a local breastfeeding group. Save the number in your phone before the 2 a.m. moment when you need it, because searching for help mid-crisis is miserable. If you plan to use formula, choose one, learn safe preparation, and keep a small backup supply. Feeding often takes a week or two to settle, so early support tends to matter more than the perfect plan.

Sleep needs a plan too, because newborns eat around the clock and two exhausted adults help nobody. If you have a partner, talk through shifts: one common pattern is one adult covering roughly 9 p.m. to 2 a.m. and the other 2 a.m. to 7 a.m., with the off-duty person sleeping somewhere quiet. Bottle feeds of expressed milk or formula can make shifts possible; so can having the on-duty partner handle diapers, settling, and bringing the baby to feed. Single parents can plan a rotation of overnight help for a few key nights. Aim for each adult to get one protected stretch of sleep in every 24 hours.

Stock the house by week 38

Aim to have supplies for you, not just the baby, in the house by week 38, since full-term babies arrive on their own schedule. For your own recovery, most people want: heavy absorbency pads for several weeks of bleeding, a peri bottle for rinsing, comfortable high-waisted underwear, loose clothes, nipple care items if you plan to breastfeed, a large water bottle, and easy one-handed snacks. Ask your provider at a third trimester visit what they suggest for pain relief and bowel comfort after delivery, so the right options are already in the cabinet. Put everything in one basket by the bed or the bathroom.

Then work on the freezer. A realistic target is 10 to 14 meals, enough to cover dinners for about two weeks, plus breakfast items like muffins or overnight oats. Cook double portions of things you already make and freeze half; that fills a freezer faster than a dedicated cooking weekend. Label everything with the date and reheating instructions so a helper can serve it without asking you. Round out the plan with pantry staples, paper plates for the first weeks, and a standing grocery delivery order. Food you do not have to think about is one of the most useful gifts you can give your future self.

Book your checkups and plan a mental health check-in

Your own medical follow-up belongs on the calendar before you deliver. Guidance from ACOG recommends contact with your maternity care provider within the first 3 weeks after birth, followed by ongoing care as needed and a comprehensive postpartum visit by 12 weeks. Call your clinic in the third trimester and book both, because new parents reliably schedule the baby's appointments and skip their own. Between visits, do not wait for a booked appointment if warning signs appear: call 911 or go to the emergency room for chest pain, trouble breathing, seizures, or thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, and call your provider the same day for heavy bleeding, a fever of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher, a severe headache that does not go away, or pain or swelling in one leg.

Finish the plan with a mental health check-in you agree to in advance. Mood swings, tears, and irritability in the first days, often called the baby blues, typically peak around days 2 to 5 and fade within about two weeks. Because it is hard to judge your own mood while sleep deprived, choose one person now, a partner, friend, or family member, and agree that they will ask how you are really doing at the end of each week and that you will answer honestly. If low mood, anxiety, or feeling disconnected lasts beyond two weeks or gets worse, contact your provider. That is a treatable medical issue, not a personal failing.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Postpartum care includes physical recovery, mood, sleep, feeding, contraception, chronic conditions, and practical support: not only a single six-week visit. Planning help, follow-up, transport, meals, and warning-sign awareness before birth can reduce avoidable strain.

Recovery differs after vaginal and cesarean birth. Heavy bleeding, severe pain, wound concerns, high blood pressure symptoms, and mental-health changes require timely assessment.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to organize support contacts, appointments, medicines, feeding questions, and recovery notes. The app is not a postpartum triage or crisis service.

When to seek help

Seek urgent care for heavy bleeding, chest pain, trouble breathing, severe headache, fever, seizures, thoughts of harm, or another urgent maternal warning sign.

Evidence notes updated: August 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Write a one-page postpartum plan in the third trimester, the counterpart to your birth plan.
  • Turn vague offers of help into named jobs, and set visitor rules with your partner in advance.
  • Save a lactation support contact and agree on a sleep shift plan before the birth.
  • Stock recovery supplies and about two weeks of freezer meals by week 38.
  • Book a postpartum check within 3 weeks of birth and a comprehensive visit by 12 weeks, before you deliver.

Frequently asked questions

How do I prepare for postpartum before the baby arrives?

Write a one-page plan in the third trimester covering support, feeding, sleep, supplies, meals, and your own medical follow-up. Assign named helpers to specific jobs, save a lactation contact, stock recovery supplies by week 38, and book your postpartum visits before delivery. A short written plan beats a long mental one, because the early weeks leave little room for decisions.

When should I schedule my postpartum checkup?

Book it before you deliver: ACOG recommends contact with your provider within the first 3 weeks after birth and a comprehensive postpartum visit by 12 weeks. Many clinics let you schedule both during a third trimester appointment. If you had a complicated pregnancy or delivery, your provider may want to see you sooner, so ask what timing fits your situation.

What are the postpartum essentials for mom?

The core postpartum essentials for mom are heavy absorbency pads, a peri bottle, comfortable high-waisted underwear, loose clothes, nipple care items if breastfeeding, a large water bottle, and easy one-handed snacks. Ask your provider what they recommend for pain relief and bowel comfort after delivery. Keep everything in one basket near where you plan to rest.

How many freezer meals should I prep before the baby comes?

A realistic target is 10 to 14 freezer meals, roughly two weeks of dinners, plus some breakfast items. Cooking double portions of your regular meals in the last month usually gets you there without a marathon cooking day. Label each meal with the date and reheating instructions so any helper can serve it.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
